title: Continuity escalation ladder and persona messaging
body:
Purpose:
This is a working brief for GTM-facing and customer-facing messaging when inference disruptions occur or when graceful degradation policies are enacted. Goal: give the field prescriptive language and an escalation ladder that maps technical mitigations to customer-facing narratives for different personas.

Why a ladder:
- Too many incidents are handled as binary: 'all up' or 'all down'.
- Customers care about continuity of experience, not internal tech details.
- A graded ladder lets us align mitigation actions (e.g., local caching, routing to regional pool, model downgrade, response trimming) to clear communications and commitments.

Audience & personas (short):
- Product/feature PM (wants impact on UX and timeline)
- Developer/Eng (wants technical detail and workaround steps)
- Platform/SRE (needs blast radius and mitigation timeline)
- Procurement/Legal (needs SLA/credits framing for revenue requests)
- Customer success / AE (needs scripts for high-touch outreach)

Escalation ladder (technical -> comms mapping):
1) Silent mitigation (no comms):
   - Action: prefix caching, KV cache hit used, local fallbacks for short TTLs.
   - When used: micro spikes, no end-user visible failures.
   - Customer message (if asked): "We applied a short-term cache to avoid transient delays; no action required on your side."

2) Low-impact degradation (email/console note):
   - Action: smart batching increased, best-effort model quantization path, minor throughput reduction to keep latency SLOs.
   - When used: small but sustained load above predicted capacity.
   - Persona script (PM): "You may see slightly higher tokenization compression or marginally shorter outputs; quality unchanged for most calls. We're prioritizing latency; full capacity restoration expected within X hours."

3) Managed graceful degrade (targeted comms + in-console banner):
   - Action: route non-critical traffic to lower-cost model variants; apply response length caps for non-essential routes; enable partial streaming.
   - When used: prolonged capacity pressure or region-specific resource constraints.
   - AE script: "We're serving a compatible model variant for non-sensitive traffic to maintain availability. For your premium routes, we're activating reserved capacity to preserve full fidelity."

4) Regional fallback (multi-region failover):
   - Action: route requests to alternate region; escalate to cross-region capacity; synchronize KV cache where possible; degrade analytics granularity.
   - When used: region outage, network partition, localized DC failure.
   - Customer comms template: "We've shifted your workload to Region B to maintain availability. There may be a transient increase in latency and logging differences; your data residency settings remain enforced via VPC peering and KMS controls."

5) Major outage (incident comms, daily updates):
   - Action: enable emergency autoscale/fallback pool, prioritize core routes, manual sharding of traffic, sales-led executive outreach.
   - Comms cadence: initial acknowledgement within 30 minutes, follow-ups at predictable intervals (1h, 3h, 6h), and a postmortem within 72 hours.

Incident narrative templates (short form):
- Initial ack (public-facing): "We are investigating increased error rates affecting model inference in Region X. Our engineers are working to restore normal service. Impacted features: [list]. We will provide updates at regular intervals."
- Technical update (developer-facing): "Root cause appears to be throttling in GPU host pool due to a replicated scheduler bug. Mitigation applied: temporary routing to variant fleet + cache warm; error rate dropped from 6% to 1.2%. Next steps: deploy scheduler patch and validate canary."
- Executive outreach (customer success): "We understand this impacts your SLA. We've prioritized your critical routes and expect to restore full fidelity by [ETA]. We're prepared to offer consumption credits per our SLA if we miss the target."

Competitive notes (differentiation opportunities):
- Most competitors default to 'single-model fallback' or 'queue until capacity frees' — both create poor UX or long tail latency.
- Differentiator: our policy toolbox (region+model+cache+response-trim) + predictable comms cadence = perceived continuity.
- Sales angle: emphasize predictable economics (we can cap cost of emergency capacity) and a defined escalation ladder — not just an apology.

Trust language guidelines (short list):
- Be specific about impact (which API routes, what % of requests, sample error codes).
- Say what we are doing (actions) and when we will next update (cadence).
- Commit to a post-incident summary with root cause and remediation plan; avoid speculative causes before RCA.
- Offer clear remediation/compensation pathways tied to SLA language.

Examples:
- Bad: "We experienced an outage. Sorry."
- Better: "A subset of inference requests returned 503 between 10:17–10:42 UTC due to scheduler backpressure; we routed to a fallback fleet and error rate reduced to <1%. Next update 11:30 UTC; full postmortem by 2025-02-20."

Operational playbook snippets (for SRE + AE):
- Triage checklist: assess scope -> select ladder step -> pick comms template -> identify exec customers -> set update cadence -> open RCA ticket.
- Who to notify: product PM, SRE lead, AE for affected accounts, CSM for high-touch accounts.

Field-facing scripts (short):
- For developer portal banner: "Intermittent inference errors in Region X. We're applying a compatibility fallback to keep requests served. Expect occasional shorter outputs and slight latency differences. Follow status.redwood.ai for updates."
- For partner status page: "Traffic rerouted to alternate region due to localized capacity issue. No data loss; some routes may experience increased latency."

Metrics to track during ladder activation:
- error_rate by route
- 95th and 99th latency
- cache_hit_ratio for prefix caching
- model_variants_percent (how much traffic on downgraded variants)
- percentage of critical routes impacted

Open questions / decisions to bake into product:
- Default comms cadence per ladder step (do we standardize times for all customers or tier by SLAs?).
- How to present 'degraded but available' in our billing UI and invoices.
- Which automated flags should trigger AE/CSM notifications vs. only console messages?

Next actions (work items):
- Draft templated email sequences for steps 2–5 (owner: Marcus Chen)
- Add ladder states to incident runbook UI (owner: SRE product)
- Sales enablement 1-pager with example scripts and competitive talking points (owner: Lena Morales)
- Run 1 tabletop with sample customer personas to validate scripts (owner: Aisha Patel)

Notes to self / rough brainstorm lines:
- Consider a customer-configurable ladder where enterprise customers can pin 'no-downgrade' routes to reserved capacity automatically.
- For private deployments, emphasize control plane vs data plane behaviors; comms need to avoid implying Redwood has access to on-prem data.
- Explore short URLs for canned responses so AEs can paste into tickets rapidly (e.g., tiny.redwood/region-fallback).

References & anchors: link to internal playbook and incident templates (see linked_artifacts).

Status: this is a draft — leaning toward a single canonical ladder but with per-SLA overrides. Feedback requested from SRE and AE teams on wording and timing expectations.
